messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ricardo, a 62-year-old dancer, had always moved through the world with a fluid grace that belied his age, until the night seven months ago when his life irrevocably fractured. Driving home after a late rehearsal, a drunk driver swerved into his lane, the screech of tires and the sickening crunch of metal echoing in his mind long after the collision. He was trapped, the smell of burning rubber and shattered glass thick in the air, the frantic shouts of first responders blending with the blare of sirens. He remembered the searing pain, the feeling of being utterly helpless as his body, his instrument, was mangled within the wreckage.

In the months that followed, the memory of that night refused to settle into a coherent narrative. Ricardo found himself unable to put the frightening event into words, the experience remaining a raw, unarticulated terror. Instead, when he had memories of what happened, he would often hear fragments of the collision in his head — the metallic shriek, the breaking glass, the urgent, unintelligible voices — a relentless auditory recall that would pierce his quiet moments. Each time these sounds erupted, an intense shame would flood him, a burning humiliation for his vulnerability, for the violence inflicted upon him. To escape this visceral shame and the intrusive auditory recall, Ricardo would immediately try hard to suppress thoughts about the trauma, pushing them away with all his might. He also began to deliberately try to leave his body or blank out, a dissociative strategy that offered a momentary, albeit unsettling, reprieve from the overwhelming feelings. This constant mental effort to disconnect also extended to his nights; he would stay up until very late, dreading the vivid nightmares that plagued the few hours of sleep he did manage to get.

These maladaptive strategies, while offering fleeting relief, ultimately tightened the grip of his distress. By constantly trying to suppress his thoughts and deliberately dissociate, Ricardo had come to believe that he would never be able to feel normal emotions again, convinced that his capacity for joy and connection had been permanently severed. This profound sense of lost emotions, combined with a growing conviction that the event happened to him because of the sort of person he was—a subtle, insidious form of character blame—fed a pervasive sense of threat. He experienced strong negative emotions, primarily fear and horror, almost constantly, his body keyed up for danger. When he entered any room, even his familiar dance studio, his eyes would immediately scan for exits, a desperate, unconscious search for an escape route. This hypervigilance made him jumpy; if his wife, Elena, touched him unexpectedly, he would react with alarm, his muscles tensing, his breath catching.

This persistent state of heightened threat, the constant fear and the automatic scanning for exits, served to reinforce his negative appraisals. Every time he startled or felt the surge of panic, it solidified his belief that he couldn't stop bad things from happening to him, confirming his profound sense of helplessness. The feeling of being perpetually unsafe also deepened his conviction that he was fundamentally flawed, a belief that fed back into his character blame. The constant internal alarm also made his memories of the collision more vivid and distressing. The auditory recall of the screeching tires and the shouts of paramedics became louder, more insistent, triggered by the slightest perceived danger, pulling him back into the shame and horror of the event.

Ricardo's life, once defined by movement and expression, was now shrinking. His attempts to suppress thoughts and delay sleep left him perpetually exhausted, affecting his ability to focus during rehearsals. His need to scan for exits made it difficult to lose himself in the flow of a performance, always half-present. The physical demands of partner work became fraught with anxiety, as his tendency to startle to touch made intimate contact with other dancers, and with Elena, a source of tension rather than connection. Elena, deeply concerned by his increasing withdrawal and the visible toll of his sleeplessness, finally convinced him to seek help. Ricardo came to therapy feeling a profound despair, afraid that this fearful, disconnected version of himself was now permanent, and that the vibrant dancer he once was had been lost forever.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not convey that Ricardo's maladaptive strategies influence or lead to his trauma memory.
